name: Changunarayan
tagline: A hilltop Vishnu temple with Nepal's oldest dated inscription
meta_description: Changunarayan with locals: the 464 CE Licchavi pillar, Vishnu sculptures, the village, and walks to Bhaktapur and from Nagarkot. Fees, timing, transport.
summary: Changunarayan is a hilltop temple of Vishnu above the Manohara river, about 7 km north of Bhaktapur. In its courtyard stands a pillar inscribed by King Manadeva in 464 CE, Nepal's oldest dated inscription, and some of the finest Licchavi stone sculpture in the valley. Allow half a day, ideally with a walk.
intro: Changunarayan sits at the end of a long ridge on the north-east side of the valley, with a small Newar village climbing the hill below it. A single cobbled street of brick houses and craft shops leads up to the temple gate. Step inside and you enter a courtyard that has been sacred for over 1,500 years, crowded with stone sculptures, shrines and bells.

The two-roofed pagoda at the centre is dedicated to Vishnu as Narayan. It was rebuilt after a fire in the early 18th century, and its struts, doors and gilded windows are among the richest in the valley. But the real treasures are older: a stone pillar inscribed in 464 CE by the Licchavi king Manadeva, and stone images of Vishnu carved in the same era, which shaped temple art across Nepal.

Changunarayan is part of the Kathmandu Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site, yet it is much quieter than the Durbar Squares. Most visitors combine it with Bhaktapur, a 2-hour walk downhill, or with Nagarkot, from where a ridge path leads down through villages and forest. Come in the morning for local worship and soft light on the stones.

story.title: Manadeva's pillar and the Licchavi kings
paras: The Licchavi kings ruled the valley from roughly the 4th or 5th to the 9th century CE, and Changunarayan is one of their most important surviving sites. In 464 CE King Manadeva set up a stone pillar here with a long Sanskrit inscription. It records how, after his father King Dharmadeva died, his mother wished to follow her husband in death, and Manadeva persuaded her to live.

The inscription is the oldest dated one known in Nepal and a key source for the history of the period. Around it, Licchavi sculptors carved Vishnu in his many forms: as Trivikrama striding across the universe, as the many-headed Vishwarupa, and as the man-lion Narasimha. A kneeling Garuda, Vishnu's mount, faces the temple door, and local tradition holds that its face is a portrait of Manadeva.

The temple itself has been rebuilt several times, most notably in the early 18th century after a fire. In 2015 the earthquake damaged the temple and destroyed many houses in the village below. The main temple has since been repaired, and the village has been rebuilt with help from heritage groups and residents. The stones of the courtyard, however, have stood through it all.

legend: Local legend says a cowherd's cow went each day to a champak tree on this hill and poured her milk at its roots. Her Brahmin owner, suspecting something evil in the tree, cut it down. Blood flowed from the trunk, and Vishnu appeared. He told the Brahmin that the blow had freed him from an old sin, and the place became sacred. The temple of Changu Narayan was raised where the tree stood.
people: Changu village is Newar, with families of farmers, shopkeepers and craftsmen who look after the temple and run small guesthouses and shops along the main street. Priests serve the temple daily. Below the hill, villages of Newar, Brahmin and Chhetri farmers grow rice, wheat and vegetables on the terraces above the Manohara river. Many families sell thangkas, masks and carvings to visitors.

untold.fact: The stone pillar at Changunarayan, inscribed by King Manadeva in 464 CE, is the oldest dated inscription found in Nepal. It tells how he talked his widowed mother out of following his father in death.
Changunarayan is one of the seven monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site, and is often described as one of the oldest temple sites in the valley.
untold.source: UNESCO World Heritage listing: Kathmandu Valley

untold.fact: In the courtyard, a 7th-century stone sculpture of Vishnu riding Garuda, known as Garuda Narayan or Chanda Narayan, is among the finest early carvings in Nepal. The kneeling Garuda before the temple door has a human face.

local_words.meaning: A name of Vishnu, preserver of the universe
Garuda, the bird-man who carries Vishnu

taste.name: Gwaramari
taste.text: A round Newar breakfast bread of spiced flour batter, deep fried until puffed and crisp outside and soft inside, eaten with milk tea. Tea shops along Changu's main street and in Bhaktapur fry them in the morning. Order a couple before setting off on the walk down.

facts: 464 CE inscription, Licchavi sculpture, hill walks

highlights.title: Manadeva's pillar
highlights.text: The stone pillar of 464 CE stands near the temple's western door, its Sanskrit lines still visible. It is Nepal's oldest dated inscription and a direct line back to the Licchavi kings.

highlights.title: Licchavi Vishnu sculptures
highlights.text: Stone images of Vishnu as Trivikrama, Vishwarupa and Narasimha, among the finest early sculpture in Nepal. Look closely at the detail of faces, hands and garments carved over 1,000 years ago.

highlights.title: The kneeling Garuda
highlights.text: Facing the main door, the bird-man Garuda kneels with hands joined. Local tradition says his face is a portrait of King Manadeva, which would make it one of the earliest royal likenesses in the valley.

highlights.title: Changu village
highlights.text: A short cobbled street of brick houses, small museums, thangka shops and tea stalls leads up to the temple. Rebuilt after 2015, it is quiet and friendly, with views over the valley.

highlights.title: Walk down to Bhaktapur
highlights.text: From the temple, a path leads down through terraces and across the Manohara river to Bhaktapur, about 2 hours. A classic half-day pairing of two UNESCO zones on foot.

how_to_reach.text: Changunarayan is about 22 km east of central Kathmandu and 7 km north of Bhaktapur. A taxi or private car takes about an hour from Thamel, or 20 to 30 minutes from Bhaktapur. Local buses run from Bhaktapur to Changu village. Cars stop at the foot of the village street.

From Bhaktapur, walk up via the Manohara river and terraced fields in about 2 to 2.5 hours. From Nagarkot, a longer walk via Telkot along the ridge takes 3 to 4 hours, mostly downhill through forest and villages.

where_to_stay: A few small guesthouses in Changu village and on the ridge offer simple rooms with valley views, good for a quiet night away from the city. Most travellers visit as a half-day trip and stay in Bhaktapur's old town, 30 minutes away, or at Nagarkot, where Club Himalaya and other hotels face the mountains. Combining a Nagarkot night with a walk down to Changunarayan and Bhaktapur works well.
tips: Foreign visitors pay an entry fee at the gate to the village; keep the ticket.
Only Hindus may enter the inner sanctum, but the courtyard and its sculptures are open to all.
Go in the morning for local worship and soft light, before day groups arrive.
Wear good shoes for the walk down to Bhaktapur, which has steep, uneven stone sections.
Bring a small torch or use your phone light to read the inscription in the shade.

experiences.title: Read Changunarayan's Licchavi stones with a guide
experiences.summary: A close look at the temple courtyard with a guide who knows its sculptures: Manadeva's 464 CE pillar, the kneeling Garuda, and Licchavi images of Vishnu as Trivikrama, Vishwarupa and Narasimha. Learn to read a temple strut and see why this site matters to Nepal's history.
body: We enter the courtyard by the main gate and start with the temple itself, a two-roofed pagoda rebuilt in the early 18th century. Its struts show the many forms of Vishnu and other deities, and its gilded doors and windows are decorated with mythical creatures. Your guide explains how to read the struts from bottom to top.

Then we turn to the older stones. Near the western door stands the pillar of King Manadeva, dated 464 CE, with its Sanskrit text recording how he persuaded his mother not to follow his father in death. In front of the main door, Garuda kneels with joined hands. Tradition says his face is Manadeva's.

Around the courtyard we look at Licchavi carvings of Vishnu: Trivikrama striding across the worlds, the many-armed Vishwarupa, and Narasimha tearing apart the demon king. We also see later shrines to Chhinnamasta, Lakshmi and Shiva. The tour ends with time to sit and watch villagers making their morning offerings.

faqs.q: Why is Changunarayan temple important?
faqs.a: It is one of the oldest temple sites in the Kathmandu Valley and holds Nepal's oldest dated inscription, carved for King Manadeva in 464 CE. Its courtyard has some of the finest Licchavi stone sculpture in Nepal. It is one of the seven monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site.

faqs.q: How much is the Changunarayan entry fee?
faqs.a: Foreign visitors pay an entry fee of a few hundred rupees at the gate to the village; SAARC nationals pay less and Nepalis enter free. The ticket covers the temple courtyard. Fees change, so check current status before you travel and carry rupees in cash.

faqs.q: Can non-Hindus enter Changunarayan temple?
faqs.a: Non-Hindus can enter the courtyard and see all the sculptures, the inscription and the temple exterior. Only Hindus may enter the inner sanctum where the main image is kept. Remove shoes where signs ask, and do not touch offerings.

experiences.title: Walk from Changunarayan down to Bhaktapur
experiences.summary: After the temple, walk down through Changu village, terraced fields and small settlements, cross the Manohara river and enter Bhaktapur's old town from the north. About 7 km, mostly downhill, ending with juju dhau in Taumadhi.
body: From the temple gate, we walk down Changu's cobbled street and leave the village on a path that drops through terraced fields. In autumn the rice is golden and being cut; in spring, wheat and mustard fill the terraces. Farmers often stop to chat, and children call out from doorways.

The path descends steadily for about an hour to the Manohara river, which we cross by a bridge. On the far side, we walk through fields and the edges of new suburbs towards Bhaktapur, with views back up to the Changunarayan ridge. The path is steep and uneven in places, so take it slowly.

We enter Bhaktapur's old town from the north, through quiet residential lanes, and finish at Taumadhi or the Durbar Square, where you can buy your Bhaktapur ticket and sit down for a well-earned bowl of juju dhau. Your driver meets you here if you are not staying the night.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from Changunarayan to Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: About 7 km and 2 to 2.5 hours, mostly downhill through terraced fields and villages, crossing the Manohara river. It is easy to moderate, with some steep and uneven sections near the top. Allow extra time for photos and tea stops.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for the Changunarayan to Bhaktapur walk?
faqs.a: Not legally, but the route has several junctions and few signs, and a guide makes it easy and explains the villages. With a map app and a sense of direction, independent walkers can manage. Start in the morning to avoid afternoon heat and haze.

faqs.q: Can children do the Changunarayan walk?
faqs.a: Yes, most children over about 7 who are used to walking manage it, since it is mostly downhill. Steep, loose sections near the top need care. Carry water and snacks, and arrange a car to pick up at Bhaktapur for tired legs.

experiences.title: Nagarkot to Changunarayan along the ridge
experiences.summary: After a Nagarkot sunrise, walk west along the ridge via Telkot through pine forest and villages, then down to Changunarayan. About 12 km, mostly downhill, with mountain views early and the Licchavi temple at the end. A classic valley day hike.
body: We start after breakfast at Nagarkot, around 2,100 m, and follow the ridge west. The first stretch passes through pine forest and small Tamang and Brahmin-Chhetri settlements, with views back to the snow peaks on clear mornings. The path is broad and easy to follow with a guide.

After about 2 hours we reach Telkot, a junction village on the road, where we stop for tea. From here the route drops along a quieter ridge through fields and scattered houses, with the Kathmandu Valley opening up ahead. The descent is steady, with a few steep sections on loose ground.

We arrive at Changunarayan from above, through the back of the village, and visit the temple and its Licchavi sculptures with fresh legs and a sense of how isolated it once was. From here, continue on foot to Bhaktapur for a long day, or meet your car for the drive back to Kathmandu.

faqs.q: How long is the Nagarkot to Changunarayan hike?
faqs.a: About 12 km and 4 to 5 hours, mostly downhill, from around 2,100 m at Nagarkot to about 1,540 m at Changunarayan, via Telkot. It is easy to moderate for regular walkers. Adding the walk to Bhaktapur makes a full day of 6 to 7 hours.

faqs.q: Is the Nagarkot to Changunarayan trail well marked?
faqs.a: Partly. Some sections follow roads and are obvious, but village paths and junctions are not well signed. A guide or a good offline map is recommended. Start early to have time for tea stops and the temple visit.

faqs.q: What is the best season for the Nagarkot to Changunarayan hike?
faqs.a: October to April is best, with dry trails and clear mountain views in the morning, especially October to February. Monsoon months make paths muddy and slippery, with leeches in forest sections and few views. Start early in any season.

experiences.title: Changu village, its museums and tea shops
experiences.summary: Explore the short cobbled street below the temple: rebuilt brick houses, small family-run museums of farming tools, coins and household objects, thangka studios, and tea shops with views over the valley. Gentle and unhurried.
body: Changu village is a single main street of brick houses climbing to the temple, with lanes and courtyards branching off. Much of it was badly damaged in 2015, and many houses have been rebuilt with traditional brick and carved windows. Walking up slowly, you see the mix of old and new, and families back in their homes.

Small museums run by local families display everyday objects from Newar life: farming tools, kitchen pots, old coins, jewellery and ritual items. They are modest but give a good sense of how people lived here before roads arrived. Fees are small and go to the families.

Along the street, thangka painters and mask makers work in small studios, and tea shops offer seats with views over the terraced hills. We end with milk tea and gwaramari or a plate of beaten rice and pickles, before visiting the temple or heading down to Bhaktapur.

faqs.q: Is Changunarayan village worth exploring?
faqs.a: Yes. Most visitors walk straight up to the temple, but the village has small family museums, craft studios and tea shops with valley views. It shows how a hilltop Newar community lives and how it rebuilt after 2015. Allow an hour to wander.

faqs.q: Are there places to eat in Changunarayan?
faqs.a: Yes, a few tea shops and small restaurants along the main street serve tea, snacks, dal bhat and Newar dishes. Choices are simple. For more variety, eat in Bhaktapur, 20 to 30 minutes by car or 2 hours on foot.

faqs.q: Was Changunarayan damaged in 2015?
faqs.a: Yes. The temple was damaged and many houses in the village below collapsed. The temple has been repaired and much of the village rebuilt, with help from residents, heritage groups and donors. Some construction may still be visible.

faqs.q: How far is Changunarayan from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: About 22 km east of central Kathmandu, taking about an hour by car. It is 7 km north of Bhaktapur, a 20 to 30 minute drive or a 2-hour walk. Local buses run from Bhaktapur to Changu. Most visitors combine it with Bhaktapur or Nagarkot.

faqs.q: How old is Changunarayan temple?
faqs.a: The site is very old: its stone pillar is dated 464 CE, and Licchavi sculptures in the courtyard are well over a thousand years old. The current pagoda was rebuilt in the early 18th century after a fire, and repaired after the 2015 earthquake.

faqs.q: What is the 464 CE inscription at Changunarayan?
faqs.a: It is a Sanskrit inscription on a stone pillar set up by the Licchavi king Manadeva. It tells how, after his father's death, he persuaded his mother not to follow her husband in death. It is the oldest dated inscription found in Nepal.

faqs.q: How long should I spend at Changunarayan?
faqs.a: One to two hours covers the temple courtyard and village. Allow half a day if you walk down to Bhaktapur, or most of a day if you hike from Nagarkot. Staying overnight in a village guesthouse gives a peaceful evening and morning.

faqs.q: Is Changunarayan part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site?
faqs.a: Yes. It is one of the seven monument zones that make up the Kathmandu Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site, along with the three Durbar Squares, Swayambhu, Boudhanath and Pashupati. It is the least visited of the seven, which makes it peaceful.

faqs.q: Can I combine Changunarayan, Nagarkot and Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: Yes. A popular plan is a night at Nagarkot for sunrise, a ridge hike to Changunarayan, then the walk down to Bhaktapur for the evening. By car, you can visit all three in one long day, though walking shows the land between them.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Changunarayan?
faqs.a: October to April, especially October to February, when skies are clear, paths are dry and walks are pleasant. Visit in the morning for local worship and soft light. Monsoon months are wet and hazy, but the temple is quiet.

faqs.q: Is Changunarayan suitable for older travellers?
faqs.a: Yes, by car. Cars stop at the foot of the village, and a short, moderately steep cobbled street leads to the temple, about 10 minutes at an easy pace. The courtyard is flat. The walks to Bhaktapur or from Nagarkot are better for those with good knees.

faqs.q: Who is worshipped at Changunarayan?
faqs.a: Vishnu, in his form as Narayan, is the main deity. The courtyard also has shrines to Lakshmi, Shiva, Chhinnamasta and other gods. Garuda, Vishnu's mount, kneels before the main door. Both Hindus and many Buddhists in the valley visit the temple.
